walkthroughs.body_html:
Bonding & Structure — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Bonding & Structure brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Bonding & Structure.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which molecule has a dative covalent bond?
options: CH₄
H₂O
NH₄⁺
O₂

mcqs.q: Where is almost all the mass of an atom located?
options: In the nucleus, made up of protons and neutrons.
Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.
Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.
Electrons contribute significantly to the mass of an atom.

mcqs.q: What is different between two isotopes of the same element?
options: Because d orbitals can only fill after p orbitals in the next shell.
They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Isotopes have different numbers of electrons, which is why their mass differs.
Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.

mcqs.q: Why is the 4s orbital filled before the 3d orbital?
options: Because the 4s orbital has a lower energy than 3d when both are empty, so electrons fill it first.
Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.
Because d orbitals can only fill after p orbitals in the next shell.
Because the 4s shell is closer to the nucleus than the 3d shell.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Bond polarity”?
options: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
Unequal sharing of electrons between atoms of different electronegativity, producing δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges.
Shared pair of electrons between two atoms, often between non-metals.
Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and adopt positions maximising separation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “VSEPR theory”?
options: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and adopt positions maximising separation.
Both shared electrons originate from the same atom, e.g. NH₄⁺.
Shared pair of electrons between two atoms, often between non-metals.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Covalent bonding”?
options: Attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons.
Unequal sharing of electrons between atoms of different electronegativity, producing δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges.
Shared pair of electrons between two atoms, often between non-metals.
Both shared electrons originate from the same atom, e.g. NH₄⁺.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Ionic bonding”?
options: Shared pair of electrons between two atoms, often between non-metals.
Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and adopt positions maximising separation.
Both shared electrons originate from the same atom, e.g. NH₄⁺.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Dative covalent bond”?
options: Attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
Both shared electrons originate from the same atom, e.g. NH₄⁺.
Unequal sharing of electrons between atoms of different electronegativity, producing δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Metallic bonding”?
options: Both shared electrons originate from the same atom, e.g. NH₄⁺.
Shared pair of electrons between two atoms, often between non-metals.
Unequal sharing of electrons between atoms of different electronegativity, producing δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges.
Attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons.
